prompt: What does a model's context window have to hold?
hint: Look at why the second request was refused.

choices.text: Only the prompt, since the reply is written somewhere else
choices.why: The reply is written into the same window, token by token.

choices.text: The prompt and the reply together
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The reply only; the prompt is read before the window opens
choices.why: The prompt is the first thing in the window.

choices.text: Whatever the provider decides on the day, depending on load
choices.why: The window is a published limit of the model.

prompt: `window.py 10` found the password and `window.py 12` answered `'shop'`. What happened to the twelve-copy request?
hint: Compare what was sent with what was read.

choices.text: It was refused with an error, and the SDK made up an answer
choices.why: An error would have raised an exception; it ended with `end_turn`.

choices.text: The model ran out of `max_tokens` before reaching the password
choices.why: It answered in one word, well inside its twenty.

choices.text: Ollama dropped the start of the prompt to fit the window
choices.why: Right: about 4,512 sent, 2,050 read, and the password was at the start.

choices.text: Twelve copies confused the model with repeated text
choices.why: Ten copies of the same text did not; the difference is what was read.

prompt: `window.py 10` read 3,829 tokens and allowed 20 of output. How many tokens of Ollama's 4,096-token window were left over?

A teammate proposes sending the whole repository, 600,000 tokens, with every question, since the model's window is a million. Which objection does the section give that a bigger window would not remove?

choices.text: It will be refused, since a window that large is never offered
choices.why: The sheet lists windows of a million and more.

choices.text: The tokenizer cannot handle files of that size
choices.why: Size is not a tokenizer's problem.

choices.text: Information in the middle of a long context is used worse than at the ends
choices.why: Right, and the cost and the wait remain too.

choices.text: Repositories cannot be sent as text
choices.why: They can; `cache.py` sends one.

prompt: `tiktoken` counted 15 tokens for the question and the model read 40. Where does most of the difference come from?

choices.text: The chat template wrapped around the message
choices.why: Right: headers, and a line with the training cutoff, on every request.

choices.text: `tiktoken` drops punctuation, so it always counts low
choices.why: It counts every character; the question's `?` is a token.

choices.text: The one token of reply was counted as input
choices.why: `max_tokens=1` adds one token of output, not twenty-five of input.

choices.text: The question was translated before it was read
choices.why: Nothing translates anything.

prompt: How many tokens did one tool definition add to the question in `count.py`?
You need the token count a provider will bill for a request to a model whose tokenizer is not published. Which is it?

choices.text: `tiktoken` with `o200k_base`, since every provider uses it
choices.why: Only OpenAI's models are mapped to it.

choices.text: The number of words times 1.3
choices.why: A ratio is a guess that moves with language and subject.

choices.text: The provider's counting endpoint, or `usage` on the response
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The length in characters divided by four
choices.why: Same problem as any ratio.

prompt: Why log `usage` on every call from the first day?
hint: What question does the bill raise?

choices.text: The provider deletes it after an hour
choices.why: It is in the response; the point is keeping it.

choices.text: To split the bill by feature later
choices.why: Right. Only per-request usage answers which feature spent it.

choices.text: Because the SDK refuses to run without a logger
choices.why: The SDK has no such rule.

choices.text: To retrain the model on your traffic
choices.why: Usage is a count, not training data.

prompt: Model prices are quoted in dollars per million tokens, written `$` per ___.
hint: Four letters, as the sheet prints them.

prompt: At Claude Sonnet 5.5's prices ($2 in, $10 out per MTok), what does a request with 4,000 tokens in and 1,000 out cost, in dollars?
Why does the price sheet carry a date beside Anthropic's prices and a commit beside the others?
hint: One source is versioned and one is not.

choices.text: So that prices older than a month can be refused
choices.why: Nothing refuses them; the date is for the reader.

choices.text: Because the law requires a date on any price
choices.why: The reason in the section is about checking a number, not law.

choices.text: Because LiteLLM's prices are always out of date
choices.why: The commit pins them; it says nothing about their age.

choices.text: A page changes in place; a commit does not
choices.why: Right. The date is part of the page's number, and the commit pins the other file.

prompt: In the sheet, which comparison shows the larger price ratio per input token?

choices.text: `gpt-5.5` against `gpt-5.4-nano`
choices.why: Right: 5 against 0.2 is 25 times.

choices.text: Claude Opus 5.5 against Claude Haiku 4.5
choices.why: 4 against 1 is four times.

choices.text: `gemini-pro-latest` against `gemini-3.5-flash`
choices.why: 2 against 1.5 is a third more.

choices.text: Claude Sonnet 5.5 against `gemini-pro-latest`
choices.why: Both are $2.

prompt: Why does `cost.py` use `Decimal` rather than `float`?
hint: The shop keeps its prices the same way, for the same reason.

choices.text: Because the SDK returns `usage` as `Decimal` and the two must match
choices.why: `usage` is integers.

choices.text: Because `float` cannot hold numbers above a million or so
choices.why: It can, but not every fraction exactly.

choices.text: Rounding errors in fractions of a cent add up over millions of requests
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because `Decimal` arithmetic is faster than `float` arithmetic
choices.why: It is slower; that is not the reason.

prompt: The request in `cost.py` was 285 tokens in, nearly all of them the cart's code, and 122 out. Which change would cut its cost most?
hint: Where are two thirds of it?

choices.text: A shorter question
choices.why: The question is about ten tokens; there is almost nothing to cut.

choices.text: A lower ceiling on the length of the answer
choices.why: Right: output is two thirds of the cost at these prices.

choices.text: Leaving the cart's code out of the request
choices.why: It is a third of the cost, and without it the answer is a guess.

choices.text: Sending it at temperature 0
choices.why: Temperature does not change the price.

prompt: At Claude Haiku 4.5's prices ($1 in, $5 out), what does a month of 1,000 requests a day cost, each 2,000 tokens in and 200 out? Take a month as 30 days.
hint: Cost of one request, times 1,000, times 30.

prompt: Which costs does the section say a first estimate leaves out? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last part of the section.

choices.text: A reply your code threw away after it was billed
choices.why: Yes: it was billed in full.

choices.text: The price per million tokens
choices.why: That is the estimate's main input.

choices.text: A conversation's history, resent every turn
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Your own tests and experiments
choices.why: Yes, which is one reason lesson 4 keeps models out of unit tests.

prompt: Turn 10's total was 6,070 tokens and turn 20's was 24,740. Why is doubling the turns roughly four times the input?

choices.text: The price per token goes up after the tenth turn
choices.why: The price per token never changes.

choices.text: The replies got longer as the conversation went on
choices.why: The reply was the same fixed text every turn.

choices.text: The cache emptied halfway through
choices.why: Cached tokens are counted in the total all the same.

choices.text: Each request carries every earlier turn
choices.why: Right, so the total grows with the square of the length.

prompt: Match each way of handling a long conversation to what it costs you.

pairs.left: Keep only the last few exchanges
pairs.right: The model forgets the oldest turns

pairs.left: Replace old turns with a summary
pairs.right: One extra request now and then

prompt: How many input tokens did all twenty requests of `conversation.py` add up to?
At Anthropic, the first request of `cache.py` would pay $2.50 per million for its 1,417 cached tokens, against $2 with no cache. Why more?

choices.text: The system prompt is counted twice when it is cached
choices.why: It is counted once, as a cache write.

choices.text: The first request of the day is billed at a higher rate
choices.why: No price depends on the time of day here.

choices.text: Writing to the cache costs more than reading with none
choices.why: Right: $2.50 against $2 per MTok, paid back only by later reads at $0.20.

choices.text: Ollama charges for the cache it keeps in memory
choices.why: Ollama charges nothing; the price is Anthropic's.

prompt: Put the parts of a request in the order that lets a cache hit most often.
trap: Putting the new question or a timestamp early is the usual slip: everything after it stops matching.

prompt: A system prompt starts with `Today is 2026-10-02 14:31:07.` and then 3,000 tokens of instructions marked for caching. The logs show cache writes on every request and no reads. Why?
hint: The cache matches from the start.

choices.text: The timestamp makes every prefix new
choices.why: Right: nothing is reused. Move it after the cached part.

choices.text: 3,000 tokens is under every provider's minimum
choices.why: Anthropic's minimum is 1,024 tokens on many models, far below 3,000.

choices.text: Caching only works for tools
choices.why: System prompts were cached in `cache.py`.

choices.text: Reads only appear after the fifth request
choices.why: A read appeared on the second in `cache.py`.

prompt: The `usage` field that shows a cache being reused starts with `cache_` and ends with `_input_tokens`. The word between them is ___.
A reply comes back with `stop_reason` set to `max_tokens`. What does that mean?

choices.text: The model finished and used exactly the room it was given
choices.why: Finishing is `end_turn`.

choices.text: It ran out of room before it had finished
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It hit one of the stop sequences
choices.why: That is `stop_sequence`.

choices.text: The provider refused to answer
choices.why: A refusal is reported differently.

prompt: A feature asks for JSON and parses the reply. What should it do when `stop_reason` is `max_tokens`?
hint: Is a cut-off JSON document JSON?

choices.text: Parse it, and fill the missing fields with defaults
choices.why: The fields that arrived may be cut too.

choices.text: Add the closing braces and parse it
choices.why: That makes a different document look complete.

choices.text: Use it if it parses
choices.why: A list cut off can still parse, and is shorter.

choices.text: Treat the call as failed
choices.why: Right: retry with more room, or report it.

choices.text: It is a waste; the section recommends the smallest value possible

prompt: A support chat sends 2,500 tokens of standing instructions, resends every past exchange, and lets replies run to 4,000 tokens. Its bill doubled in a month of steady traffic. Which change addresses the cause this lesson would look for first?
hint: Which cost grows without more users?

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens`, so fewer replies are cut off and retried
choices.why: Raising the ceiling does not lower the input.

choices.text: Cap or summarise the history, and cache the system prompt
choices.why: Right: conversations getting longer grow the input faster than linearly.

choices.text: Switch to temperature 0
choices.why: Temperature has no effect on the bill.

choices.text: Count tokens with `tiktoken` instead of the provider's endpoint
